commentaire:
(a) Time left: ~2 years until the November 2028 election, with resolution likely on election night or shortly after (or at certification in January 2029 if contested). So roughly 24–26 months of uncertainty.

(b) Status quo outcome if nothing changed: The out-party typically has an edge in an open-seat election after two terms of the same party holding the White House. Early markets (Kalshi ~65% Democratic) and the 2026 midterm environment suggest Democrats are favored. So the status quo/default lean is Democratic Party.

(c) Unexpected-outcome scenario: A Republican holds the White House for a third consecutive term — e.g., JD Vance (or Rubio) wins on a strong economy, incumbency advantage, and Democratic overreach/messaging failures, or Democrats nominate a weak/divisive candidate. "Other" would require a major third-party/independent win or an election not conducted — very unlikely but not zero given institutional stress.

Rationale: Open-seat elections after a two-term presidency historically favor the out-party, and early 2026 signals (midterm dynamics, prediction markets) tilt Democratic. But 24 months is a long horizon; fundamentals (economy, incumbency, candidate quality) can shift substantially. I put meaningful weight on Republicans given incumbency-party advantages, a potentially strong VP nominee, and the possibility Democrats nominate a polarizing figure. "Other" stays low but nonzero.

commentaire:
(a) Time left: ~23 months until FY2028 ends (Sep 30, 2028).

(b) If nothing changed: the average rate would stay near the current ~3.58% (Oct 2026 reading), drifting only slowly as existing low-coupon debt matures and is refinanced at higher rates.

(c) If the current trend continued: the average rate has been climbing steadily (~3.32% end-FY2024 → ~3.58% by Oct 2026, roughly +0.13pp/yr). Extrapolating to end-FY2028 gives roughly 3.8–3.9%.

(d) Experts/markets: CBO projects the average rate on debt held by the public hovering around 3.3–3.5% through 2028–2030 (their series is on a slightly different basis than the Treasury "total interest-bearing debt" metric, which runs a bit higher). The Treasury metric's mechanical rollover dynamic plus a modestly higher rate environment suggests a central estimate around 3.7–3.9%.

(e) Low outcome: a sharp recession forces aggressive Fed cuts, short rates fall well below 3%, and the rollover of maturing debt into cheaper coupons slows or reverses the climb — average rate stalls near 3.4–3.5%.

(f) High outcome: persistent inflation, large deficits, and elevated term premiums push new issuance coupons to 5%+, accelerating the refinancing-driven rise — average rate reaches 4.3–4.6%.

Given the mechanical, slow-moving nature of the average rate (it's a stock, not a flow), I set a fairly tight but still humble interval centered near 3.8%.
